title: Guru Ram Das close
hook: a routine, a city, and songs of longing: the fourth Guru's way

segments.voice: Yesterday, the humility of the fourth Guru: asked about his beard, he knelt to wipe a visitor's feet. Your line was humble service. Did you do the job nobody wanted, and keep quiet about it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

An alarm clock in the dark. A horse dressed for a wedding. A face you ache to see. A pool with a market at its edge. A man kneeling at a visitor's feet. Lay those on a table and they look like they belong to five different stories. They're all one Guru. All through this stretch of the path we've been listening to Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, Mahala four, and today we close his section by asking what holds those pieces together.
screen: `AN ALARM, A HORSE, A FACE.` → `A POOL, A MAN KNEELING.` → `ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Three strands run through his days on this path. The first is a routine. His salok on the Gursikh gave a clock, not a definition: rise early, make the effort, bathe, remember the Name; then, sitting and standing, with breath and mouthful, keep remembering; then help someone else remember, and the Guru asks for your dust. A day with a shape. The second strand is a city. Tradition says he set a pool, a bazaar and a sangat side by side in Ramdaspur. That's the routine given a place to live, among other people, in the middle of buying and selling. The third strand is longing. The Ghorian, the horse songs, with the body as a gift that carries the soul home. The hymn of separation in Sri Rag: the ache, the friends you ask, the sight that heals it. And in the stories, the humility of a Guru who kneels. Here's how they fit. A routine without longing can harden into a chore: the alarm, the bath, the boxes ticked. Longing without a routine can drift: a beautiful ache that never gets out of bed. And both of them, without a city, without other people, stay private. Guru Ram Das holds all three together. The longing gives the routine its warmth. The routine gives the longing somewhere to go each morning. And the city, and the kneeling, keep both of them turned toward other people. Sikh tradition says he passed the Guruship to his son Arjan, who will carry the Name into a new set of hymns. That's where we go next.
screen: `A ROUTINE: A DAY WITH A SHAPE.` · `A CITY: THE ROUTINE AMONG OTHERS.` · `LONGING: THE WARMTH INSIDE IT.` · `ALL THREE HELD TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE FOURTH GURU'S WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your morning routine, the one this week began with. In the sit, look back at the mornings since we started. Did you rise a little earlier, even once? What was the first thing you met? Don't grade it. Just choose what tomorrow's first minutes will hold, and add one thing from this week to it: a breath for someone you miss, or a moment of thanks for the horse you ride. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Guru Ram Das close. A routine, a city, and songs of longing, held together by a Guru who kneels. Today's word.
Your line: the fourth guru's way. Before you sleep tonight, set out the one thing you want to meet first tomorrow morning. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Ram Das in the morning and evening prayers that include his hymns, at his gurpurab, and at the Harmandir Sahib in the city tradition says he began.
